entities.name: French Socialist Party
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Socialist Party of France (Parti Socialiste, PS) — founded in 1905 as the Section Française de l'Internationale Ouvrière (SFIO) and refounded as the Parti Socialiste in 1969 — is one of Europe's oldest and historically most influential socialist parties, producing three French presidents (François Mitterrand 1981-1995, François Hollande 2012-2017, and the earlier history) and fundamentally reshaping France through the major reforms of Mitterrand's first term: nationalizations, the 39-hour work week, fifth week of paid vacation, abolition of capital punishment, and decentralization.

The Socialist Party's history spans the entire arc of European social democracy: the founding SFIO was one of the Second International's major parties; the 1920 Tours Congress split created the French Communist Party from the SFIO majority; León Blum's Popular Front government (1936-1938) introduced the 40-hour work week and paid vacations for French workers; post-war Socialists governed in the Fourth Republic's unstable coalitions; and Mitterrand's 1981 election represented the French left's first presidential victory since 1924, beginning a 14-year socialist presidency that dominated French politics.

The Socialist Party's modern collapse — from governing France 2012-2017 under Hollande (whose approval ratings reached 4% — the lowest in French Fifth Republic history) to near-irrelevance after Emmanuel Macron's 2017 centrist triumph, which absorbed many Socialist voters and politicians — represents one of Europe's most dramatic party collapses, mirroring the broader decline of traditional social democratic parties across Western Europe.
